Outrigger homepage: three directions

The live hero, “Set up once” and the firmware feature, rendered in today’s look and three alternatives. Same copy everywhere. Switch the theme and width to see each one in dark mode and at phone width.

Recommendation

Ship C. It keeps the Commissioner voice you like and makes the facts look measured.

Mono is reserved for numbers, units and step markers, so the page reads as more technical without getting cold.

It's also the only one small enough to land as a CSS pass on style.css without touching the copy audit.

Theme
Width

Current site

The baseline, ported rule for rule from style.css and the page's inline styles. Commissioner is a humanist sans with soft, slightly flared terminals; with the warm off-white, the 14px radius and the green numbered dots, it reads as friendly consumer hardware. That suits a first-time FM-1 owner. A firmware author sees a polished product page and has to dig to the footer to find the engineering.

Set up once

  1. Install Outrigger on your ESP32

    Plug your ESP32 into a computer and click Check my board: it says what's on the board and changes nothing. Then click Install. About two minutes, free.

    Which ESP32 do you have?

    Checking reads the board and changes nothing: nothing is installed until you confirm. Installing replaces the program only. Settings, Wi-Fi and FM-1 backups stay. No board listed?

  2. Add firmwares

    Stock V15, Felucca and Skiff come with it. Add more from the Firmware Hub's list, right on this page: Add custom firmwares.

  3. Plug everything into the hub

    From then on, everything happens on Outrigger's screen.

Installation overview

Chrome and Edge can talk to a USB device directly. Install writes Outrigger onto your ESP32's own memory, then restarts it. Nothing goes near your FM-1, and your backups are never touched.

A · Datasheet

Borrows from synth back-panels and the Espressif datasheets these people already read: a working grotesk, caps labels like silkscreen, a heavy rule over each section, figure captions, and spec rows with units. Square buttons read as hardware keys. To a firmware community it says someone measured things. Trade-offs: it is the coldest of the three, and “new best friend” sits oddly in a spec sheet. The orange is an LED colour, which means leaving brand green behind.

Copy is the live site's, unchanged. Mono labels and spec rows are a visual device built from facts already on the page, not a copy proposal.

B · Lab notebook

Mono headings on an engineering-pad grid, with steps as a checklist you tick off. It looks like a README and a build log, which is where this audience lives, and it promises you can follow along. The two Atkinson faces share bones, so mono headings and proportional text don't clash. Trade-offs: mono headlines run wide, so the h1 takes three lines on a phone. The grid adds noise behind screenshots. It risks reading as a weekend project rather than a finished tool.

Copy is the live site's, unchanged. Mono labels and spec rows are a visual device built from facts already on the page, not a copy proposal.

C · Commissioner, instrumented

Keeps Commissioner, the green and the warm voice. It cuts the radius from 14 to 8, swaps filled dots for hairline mono markers, and adds a readout strip for the numbers this crowd checks first: about two minutes to install, about a minute per switch, 100+ firmwares, and that it's free. The words stay humanist and the facts get instrument type. Trade-offs: it is the smallest change, so it makes less of a splash on announcement day. Two faces need discipline: once mono leaks into sentences, it turns into B.

Copy is the live site's, unchanged. Mono labels and spec rows are a visual device built from facts already on the page, not a copy proposal.
